sections.b: The site translates Atrahasis in full from the Akkadian, so the parallel that Genesis 1–11 is most often compared with can be read whole rather than in summaries. It is the one Babylonian poem that runs, like Genesis 1–9, from the making of humankind to the Flood and the order of life afterward (Millard). Its best copy was written at Sippar in the reign of Ammi-saduqa of Babylon; the second tablet is dated to his 11th year, about 1628 BC (SEAL). The gods make humankind from clay and a slain god's flesh and blood to carry their work basket (Atrahasis 3); the noise of humankind keeps Enlil awake (Atrahasis 5); Enki warns Atrahasis through a reed wall to build a boat (Atrahasis 10); the starving gods gather over his sacrifice like flies, and then limit human births (Atrahasis 12). The book's opening pages weigh every answer to the borrowing question, from King (1918) and von Rad to Heidel (1949), Millard (1967) and Hasel (1974), and which figures of the poem may be the same as someone in the Bible.

common: Atrahasis and Genesis 1–9 share an outline (creation of humans, trouble, flood, sacrifice, a new order), but differ in their gods, in why the Flood came, and in how the story ends.
uncommon: Albert Clay (1922) argued that the Flood story was Amorite or Hebrew in origin and was taken into Babylonia, rather than the other way round.
